::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Status: BLOCKED BY REVIEW on 2026-09-19. Do not run this.

Both reviewers returned **unsound**: three fatal findings and eleven major. Full review at
[reviews/P02](../reviews/P02.qmd).

The most concrete finding is verified and correct. **The temporal classification is wrong.**
`probes.py` compares calendar years, so every same-year match falls into pre-retraction by
default. Recounting: 83 strictly post, 66 strictly pre, and **41 same-year that the probe
reported as pre-retraction and which are actually undetermined**. Section 5 of the document
below presents 107 pre-retraction as a finding that justifies the whole design, and 41 of
those 107 are an artifact of comparing years. Retraction Watch carries full dates; PubMed often
carries only a year, so the honest fix produces three classes and not two.

The reviewers also found, independently of each other, that the comparison arm does not exist:
the document promises articles matched on journal and year, and what it actually specifies is
whatever screening excludes, with no matching ratio, no replacement rule and no weighting. And
that section 7's feasibility numbers were computed over both caches without applying this
study's own eligibility criteria, so they describe a different population from the one the
protocol defines.

Left exactly as submitted. A successor will be a new document.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What the document claimed when it was submitted

Probes PA to PC ran on 2026-09-16 against full text already cached by P01 and P01v2, so they
cost nothing to NCBI. Section 7 is written from `studies/P02-citing-retracted/out/probes.json`.

The screening gate is shared with [P01v2](P01v2-advocacy-and-practice-protocol.qmd): both
studies draw their comparison arm from the same frame and neither runs until screening
agreement is measured against the author's labels.

No exposure-by-outcome model has been fitted. Awaiting review by two models; the second is
quota-blocked until 2026-09-20.
:::

## 1. The question

Citing a retracted paper as though it still stands is a documented failure of the literature,
and meta-research is the field that documents it. Retracted randomized trials have been shown
to go on being cited uncorrected in systematic reviews and clinical guidelines (PMID 35779825),
and guidelines for low back pain have been shown to cite retracted and predatory work
(PMID 40156953).

Nobody has turned that instrument on meta-research itself. A field with domain expertise in
this exact failure, failing at the same rate as everyone else, would say something about how
far knowing a problem gets you toward avoiding it.

## 2. Hypothesis

Meta-research articles cite retracted work, after retraction, at a lower rate than a matched
comparison of articles in the same journals and years.

**Primary null.** The rate ratio is 1.

**What would falsify it.** A rate ratio at or above 1. The direction is stated because the
alternative is the interesting one.

**Prior expectation.** Nothing in the corpus estimates this, so the design has no anchor and
does not pretend to one.

## 3. Design

Cross-sectional study of reference lists. The unit of analysis is one reference; the unit of
modeling is one article, with its matchable reference count as the offset.

## 4. Sample

The same frame as P01v2: the qualified tier B blocks with every tier A PMID removed, screened
to meta-research, restricted to PMC full text. Reusing it rather than building a third
population means one screening effort, one independence argument, and one set of exclusions.

**Exposed arm**: screened meta-research articles.
**Comparison arm**: articles from the same journals and years that screening excluded, which
is to say articles that are not meta-research. This is a better comparison than a fresh PubMed
sample because it is drawn from the same query frame and differs on exactly the axis of
interest.

Both arms require a reference list in PMC. Probe PA found
4948 of the cached articles carry one.

## 5. Measurement

Retraction Watch is retrieved as an open CSV through Crossref Labs. Probe PB found
60972 distinct DOIs whose `RetractionNature` is `Retraction`;
expressions of concern and corrections are excluded because they are not retractions and
counting them would inflate every arm.

A cited DOI counts as a citation of retracted work when it appears in `OriginalPaperDOI`.

### The classification that decides the result

A reference is only a failure if the retraction preceded the citing article. Every match is
classified:

| class | meaning | probe count |
|---|---|---|
| post-retraction | the retraction predates the citing article | 83 |
| pre-retraction | the citing article came first | 107 |
| undated | no usable retraction date | 0 |

**The pre-retraction class is the majority.** 107 of
190 matches are citations of work that had not yet been
retracted, and a study that counted those as failures would report more than twice the true
rate. The probe is what establishes that; it was not assumed.

A third class, an article citing a retracted paper deliberately as an example, is separated by
the `retract` topic label and by the citation context from the surrounding sentence, and every
article carrying that label is additionally reported separately.

## 6. Outcome

Count of post-retraction citations per article, with the article's DOI-matchable reference
count as the offset.

## 7. Feasibility, computed

**Every number here is emitted by `out/probes.json`.**

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| articles with a reference list in cache | 4948 |
| total references | 268290 |
| references carrying a DOI | 222730 |
| **DOI coverage** | **83.0 percent** |
| median references per article | 46 |
| citations of retracted work, any timing | 190 |
| articles citing at least one | 152 |
| **post-retraction citations** | **83** |
| articles with at least one post-retraction citation | 70 |

DOI coverage is 83.0 percent, not the 62 percent the original one-page
proposal estimated from three articles. The earlier figure came from a sample too small to
estimate anything and is superseded.

**70 articles carry the outcome.** That is enough
to fit a count model and not enough to slice finely; the design commits to one primary
comparison and no subgroup analyses.

### A defect the probe caught

A first version computed DOI coverage as distinct DOI-like strings per article divided by the
reference count and reported **1.41**. A rate above 1 is impossible and is the only reason it
was noticed: the plain-text fallback regex matches several times inside one reference, so the
numerator was not a subset of the denominator. Coverage is now counted per reference.

## 8. Analysis

In R.

```r
glm.nb(n_post_retraction ~ arm + year_c + offset(log(n_matchable_refs)), data = d)
```

Negative binomial rather than Poisson, with the dispersion parameter reported rather than
assumed. Preregistered sensitivity analyses:

1. Excluding every article carrying the `retract` topic label from both arms.
2. Poisson with robust standard errors, to show the distributional choice is not carrying the
   result.
3. Restricted to articles published from 2015, when Retraction Watch coverage is densest.
4. Counting expressions of concern alongside retractions.

## 9. Threats, and what happened to each

| threat | what was done | removed or disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-retraction citations counted as failures | Classified by date; the probe shows they are the majority | Removed |
| Papers about retraction cite retracted work deliberately | Separated by topic label and reported separately | Disclosed |
| DOI coverage may differ between arms | Measured per arm before the model is fitted; the offset is biased if it differs | Disclosed |
| Retraction Watch is incomplete | A missing retraction biases both arms toward the null equally | Disclosed |
| Retraction dates are the database's, not always the publisher's | A late date misclassifies post as pre, in both arms | Disclosed |
| Comparison arm is defined by screening exclusion | Depends entirely on the screening gate; the study cannot run before it | Disclosed |
| Reference lists in `<back>` only | Articles whose references PMC does not structure are absent, not zero | Disclosed |

## 10. Probes

| probe | computes | goes to | what would change the design | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PA** | reference counts and DOI coverage | 7 | coverage below about 50 percent makes the offset unreliable | done |
| **PB** | raw Retraction Watch matches | 7 | fewer than about 30 matches makes the study unpowered | done |
| **PC** | the post and pre retraction split | 5, 7 | a post-retraction count under about 20 ends the study | done |
| **PD** | DOI coverage separately per arm, after screening | 9 | a differential in coverage biases the offset and needs adjustment | outstanding, needs screening |
| **PE** | screening agreement, shared with P01v2 probe P6 | 4 | below kappa 0.75 triggers the hand-screening fallback | outstanding, needs the author |

## 11. Deviations

Recorded in a `DEVIATIONS` section on the result page: what changed, when, why, and the
estimate before and after where computable.

## 12. What this cannot show

- **It is not causal.** Meta-research authors may differ from other authors in ways unrelated
  to their expertise in retraction.
- **A citation is not an endorsement.** The design counts post-retraction citations and does
  not read what each one says about the work it cites. A citation flagging a paper as retracted
  is counted as a failure unless the `retract` label catches it.
- **Retraction Watch is the ground truth and it is not.** Coverage is best for recent,
  English-language, indexed work.
